item.title: Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Every n-qubit Dicke state |Dkn⟩ can be prepared exactly without ancillary qubits in O(log⁡n) circuit depth using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs.

Grade 0.418 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Yunqi Huang, Wei Zi, Jianhao He, Zekun Ye, Shenggen Zheng

Figure

Schematic of the ancilla-free circuit architecture: coherent compression of 31-qubit blocks into 5 qubits releases 26 ancilla qubits to compute total weight and apply phase operations, which drive constant-step exact amplitude amplification.

Asks

Can every n-qubit Dicke state be prepared exactly using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs, with O(log⁡n) depth and without ancillary qubits?

Before

For balanced Dicke states, exact ancilla-free circuits required O(n2) gates and O(n) depth (Bärtschi and Eidenbenz 2019, Yuan and Zhang 2025). Polylogarithmic depth required O(nlog⁡n) ancillary qubits (Liu, Childs, and Gottesman 2024).

But

Asymptotic scaling in the circuit model with arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs; holds for any n≥2 and 1≤k≤n−1.

Tools

coherent block compression · reversible carry-save addition · weight-dependent phase correction · exact amplitude amplification

Abstract

We construct exact circuits for n-qubit Dicke states of any Hamming weight k using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs in O(logn) depth without ancillary qubits. The gate count and depth are asymptotically optimal for every 0<k<n. We compress symmetric blocks to free output qubits for weight-dependent phases. A sign correction followed by a collective rotation produces a state whose overlap with the target is at least a positive constant, so exact amplitude amplification takes O(1) steps. For balanced Dicke states (k=lfloorn/2rfloor), the logarithmic depth disproves the Ω(k) depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang (2025).

item.title: Criterion and Construction Framework for Impure Quantum (r,δ)-LRCs from Optimal (r,δ)-LRCs
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Impure quantum (r,δ)-LRCs derived from dual-containing optimal classical (r,δ)-LRCs have bounded lengths whenever d≠r+1. For d=r+1, they achieve unbounded lengths, yielding CSS and Hermitian code families with distance 2δ>r+1.

Grade 0.413 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Kun Zhou, Meng Cao

Asks

What structural condition governs whether quantum (r,δ)-LRCs derived from optimal classical (r,δ)-LRCs can be impure and have unbounded length?

Before

Impurity bounds only handled specific code families such as MP codes or J-affine variety codes, with known impure families restricted to bounded lengths HV≤q2 (Galindo et al. 2021) or non-explicit minimum distances bounded below by r+1 (Shi et al. 2024).

But

Applies to Euclidean or Hermitian dual-containing optimal classical (r,δ)-LRCs with pairwise disjoint protection codes. Code parameters require r,δ≥2 and δ<r+12.

Tools

optimal classical (r,δ)-LRC decomposition theorem · CSS construction · Hermitian construction · parity-check matrix decomposition

Abstract

This paper aims to uncover new phenomena and provide new tools for quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. The initial motivation is to identify the main reason for the existence of impure cases in such quantum codes. Our main result reveals that whether \(d = r+1\) is the key factor governing the impurity of quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. We prove that, when \(d ≠ r+1\), impure quantum codes derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs have bounded lengths. Conversely, when \(d = r+1\), we construct impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs with unbounded lengths. The central tool developed in this work is a criterion for identifying impure quantum codes derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. The main results include a criterion for impurity in quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorem 3.2), a construction framework for impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorem 4.4), and two families of impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorems 4.8 and 4.11).

item.title: Single-realization Pauli twirling for suppressing coherent error accumulation in structured quantum circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Single-realization Pauli twirling converts coherent error accumulation from Θ(L2) variance growth in bare circuits to an O(L) bound at any fixed confidence level without ensemble averaging.

Grade 0.397 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Dihang Sun, Tianqi Chen, Jin Ming Koh, Nannan Ma, Jiangbin Gong

Figure

Imbalance error |Δℐ(r)| as a function of Trotter step r for six-qubit transverse-field Ising dynamics. Bare-circuit error grows up to 9.02×10−2 (staggered state) and 1.58×10−1 (domain wall) at r=10, while Pauli twirling reduces error to 2.47×10−2 and 6.34×10−2 respectively.

Asks

Can an individual realization of a Pauli-dressed quantum circuit outperform its bare counterpart in suppressing coherent error accumulation, and under what conditions?

Before

Randomized compiling requires ensemble averaging across multiple compiled circuits to suppress coherent errors.

But

Weak coherent error regime with bounded layerwise error strengths. Twirling applies to two-qubit Clifford gates, requiring decomposition of non-Clifford blocks.

Tools

Single-qubit Pauli dressing of two-qubit Clifford gates · Connected covariance matrix diagnostic · IBM superconducting quantum processor

Abstract

Pauli twirling is conventionally understood as an ensemble-level noise-tailoring procedure which suppresses coherent components of the error channel by averaging over randomized compilations. This picture does not by itself determine whether a single realization of Pauli-dressed circuit can outperform its bare counterpart, nor does it predict when such an advantage should occur. In this work, we present single-realization based framework for the standard Pauli dressing of two-qubit Clifford gates in structured quantum circuits. This is afforded by the key insight that for weak coherent errors, the leading gate infidelity is governed by the variance of some accumulated error generator. Through both simulations and theoretical considerations, we verify that coherent errors accumulated at different entangling gates can produce Θ(L²) variance growth in a bare circuit, whereas independent Pauli dressing eliminates the cross-layer contribution on average and yields an O(L) variance bound at any fixed confidence level for a single randomly sampled realization. We then develop a covariance diagnostic that predicts when this mechanism is effective in error mitigation. We find a strong Pauli twirling advantage for coherent errors whose transported generators have large off-diagonal covariance, and little advantage when the covariance matrix is nearly diagonal. Hardware experiments on IBM superconducting processors demonstrate fidelity improvements for GHZ-state preparation and reduced observable errors in Trotterized transverse-field Ising dynamics. These results indicate that single realizations of Pauli twirling without ensemble averaging is a useful coherent-error suppression technique for structured circuits containing repeated nontrivial two-qubit operations.

item.title: Symplectic Matroids, Stabilizer Codes, and Quantum Secret-Sharing
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Every representation over any finite field of a graphical symplectic matroid for a 3-connected simple graph yields a stabilizer code of distance d=2. The dealer-shortened code recovers secret information according to pair ranks, matching mutual information I(A:d) in units of log⁡q.

Grade 0.394 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Sayantan Ganguly

Asks

Which quantum stabilizer codes and access structures are realized by graphical and Lagrangian symplectic matroids, and what polynomial determines their weight enumerators?

But

Applies to 𝔽q-linear stabilizer codes; graph representations restricted to simple graphs; uniqueness of isotropic representation holds exclusively over 𝔽2.

Tools

symplectic matroids · dealer-shortened stabilizer codes · Choi state teleportation · pair-rank formulations · weight enumerator polynomials

Abstract

An F_q-linear [[n,k]]_q stabilizer code is represented by a totally isotropic subspace of F_q²ⁿ of dimension n-k, whose full-rank generator matrix has nonzero maximal minors on admissible column sets forming the bases of a representable symplectic matroid. Sarvepalli asked whether graphical symplectic matroids introduced by Chow give stabilizer codes with good parameters, when a Lagrangian matroid induces a quantum access structure, which code realizes it, and which polynomial carries the weight enumerator. We answer these questions. For a 3-connected simple graph, every representation of a graphical symplectic matroid, over any field, gives a stabilizer code of distance exactly 2, so the girth is not a lower bound. For a represented Lagrangian matroid and a dealer, we construct the dealer-shortened stabilizer code, its logical operators, an encoding isometry and explicit recovery maps, and we show that this is the code implemented by the stabilizer state through teleportation. A set of players recovers the secret, learns nothing, or learns part of it according to a rank formula on pairs of columns, which equals its mutual information with the dealer; for graph states it becomes a cut-rank condition. Over F₂ a symplectic matroid of any rank has only one representation, so the code, its access structure and its weight enumerators depend on the matroid alone; for q≥3 even the enumerator does not. Circuit-induced authorized sets always reconstruct when the matroid is self-dual, but not in general, and a six-qubit graph state shows that the two access structures can differ even then. Finally, a polynomial in the ranks of column pairs determines both weight enumerators.

item.title: Certification of non-stabilizerness in multi-qubit systems via worst-case random access codes
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Worst-case bias of quantum and mixed-stabilizer preparations under all 4m−1 non-identity Pauli measurements both scale as 2−3m/2. Their ratio is asymptotically bounded by π/(2a∗)≲1.85, restricting magic's advantage over stabilizer mixtures to a constant factor.

Grade 0.392 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Santiago Zamora

Figure

Prepare-and-measure protocol showing certification of global 3-qubit magic using bipartite measurements whose individual reduced marginals all lie inside stabilizer polytopes.

Asks

Can non-stabilizerness in multi-qubit systems be certified via worst-case random access codes without full tomography or exponential semi-device-independent polytope complexity?

Before

Ref. [18] conjectured an upper bound of [(3+1)m−1]−1 for maximal QRAC bias; disproved here for m≥7.

But

Asymptotic regime in qubit number m; restricted to Pauli measurements for the constant-factor bound; assumes characterized or structured measurements.

Tools

worst-case random access codes · stabilizer pigeonhole criterion · Haar-random Pauli expectation integration · stabilizer polytope inradius bound

Abstract

Recent works have proposed semi-device-independent frameworks to certify non-stabilizerness, but the complexity of the stabilizer polytope makes these methods infeasible beyond a few qubits. In this work, we address this limitation by moving to partially characterized measurements in the context of worst-case random access codes. We first establish a simple condition, which we term the stabilizer pigeonhole criterion, that certifies non-stabilizerness in m-qubit pure states, and show how it can be applied to reduced states. As an application, we certify magic in W states of arbitrary size using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings. Motivated by recent work on the stabilizer marginal problem, we then construct prepare-and-measure correlations generated by global m-qubit quantum states for which every k-qubit marginal lies inside the stabilizer polytope, yet the combined correlations cannot be reproduced by any global stabilizer mixture. Finally, we derive analytical upper and lower bounds on the worst-case bias attainable with mixed stabilizer preparations in an m-qubit random access code with n Pauli measurements. For the complete set of 4^m-1 non-identity Pauli measurements, we show that the optimal quantum and mixed-stabilizer biases both scale as 2^(-3m/2), and that their ratio is asymptotically bounded by a constant (lesssim1.85), showing that in this setting, magic in the preparations alone yields at most a constant-factor advantage over stabilizer mixtures.

item.title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Ab initio construction of order n=8 Trotter-Suzuki product formulas, yielding more efficient compositions and the first generic schemes (q≥27 cycles). With ZNE mitigation at two-qubit depolarizing rate p2q=10−5, the n=8 scheme reaches minimal infidelity 0.0034% versus 0.034% for second-order Leapfrog.

Grade 0.384 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Marko Malevzivc, Johann Ostmeyer

Figure

Experimental error Errnexp. versus computational cost q/h for global and local operator groupings on an L=6 Heisenberg XZ chain. The author's recommended q=21 composition and q=30 generic schemes consistently outperform the baseline schemes by Morales et al.

Asks

Can Omelyan's direct error-term optimization approach be extended to order n=8 to derive more efficient Trotter decompositions than existing compositions of second-order schemes?

Before

Morales et al. composition schemes at order n=8.

But

Simulated quantum circuits; evaluated on 1D open-boundary Heisenberg XZ spin chains (L=6); depolarizing noise model.

Tools

Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion · free Lie algebra commutator basis · pybch · constrained numerical optimization · qiskit-omelyan

Abstract

Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order n could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond 6^th order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to 6^th order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order n = 8, and find both more efficient compositions and the first 8^th order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

item.arxave:abstract: Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order n could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond 6^th order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to 6^th order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order n = 8, and find both more efficient compositions and the first 8^th order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

item.title: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization benchmark problems from mixed Hamming packings
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Mixed Hamming packing yields a 133-instance QUBO benchmark suite (5 to 1325 variables, densities 8% to 100%) occupying a distinct region in MQLib feature space. Densely connected antiferromagnetic couplings nearly cancel local fields, leaving narrow energy margins that defeat D-Wave quantum annealers across all tested annealing times.

Grade 0.375 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Péter Naszvadi, Marcell Tukora, Roman Kuvzel, Mátyás Koniorczyk

Figure

Projection of QUBO benchmark sets onto the first two principal components of graph-theoretic features. The proposed Hamming packing instances cluster in an unoccupied feature space distinct from MQLib and existing quantum benchmarks.

Asks

Can realistic application problems from coding theory provide small yet challenging QUBO benchmarks that systematically differ from existing quantum-oriented benchmarks?

Before

Existing quantum-oriented benchmarks (tile-planting, heavy-hex instances) lie along a narrow, sparse border of the MQLib feature space, leaving the region occupied by these packing instances empty.

But

Instances restricted to 133 certified optima from mixed-integer linear programming formulations. Annealer performance evaluated only on D-Wave hardware with 500 reads per configuration up to 1000 µs.

Tools

mixed Hamming packing formulation · MQLib feature analysis and heuristics · Simulated Bifurcation Machine (SBM) · Gurobi exact solver · D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer

Abstract

Benchmarking exact solvers and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires small yet challenging instances, preferably coming from actual applications. We propose such a benchmark set derived from mixed Hamming packing, a hard problem in coding theory. Starting from its mixed-integer linear programming formulation, we provide a generator for the equivalent QUBO models and study 133 instances whose optima are certified by that formulation. In the feature space of the MQLib library, we position a broad range of existing quantum-oriented benchmarks relative to the classical ones: they lie along a narrow, sparse border of the region covered by MQLib, whereas our instances form a coherent family in a region that both collections leave almost empty. Classical heuristics and a simulated bifurcation machine find the optimum of most instances quickly, in several cases sooner than an exact mixed-integer solver first encounters it, suggesting heuristic warm starts for exact solvers; for an exact QUBO solver, in turn, it appears challenging to prove optimality. In Ising form, the instances are densely connected antiferromagnets whose large local fields are almost exactly balanced by the couplings, so that the decision on each variable rests on a small remainder. This makes them hard to embed and to represent accurately on current quantum annealers, in line with our D-Wave experiments.
